theme: David flees; Ahimelech; David at Adullam
readingInstruction: Read 1 Samuel 21:1-23:29. David is now a fugitive. Notice the mix of fear, faith, and God’s guidance in these chapters, and read the horror of chapter 22 carefully.
settingTheScene: David has escaped from Saul’s court and has nothing: no weapons, no army, and no safe place. He flees first to Nob, where the priest Ahimelech helps him, and then to Gath, to the cave of Adullam, and elsewhere. A band of distressed men gathers around him. Saul’s pursuit becomes more violent, and the priests of Nob pay a terrible price. Through it all, David inquires of the LORD and is guided.
observation: David lies to Ahimelech and receives the bread of the Presence and Goliath’s sword (21:1-9).
In Gath, David feigns madness before King Achish to escape (21:10-15).
At the cave of Adullam, “everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul, gathered to him” (22:2).
Doeg the Edomite reports David’s visit to Nob, and at Saul’s order he strikes down eighty-five priests (22:9-19).
Abiathar, one son of Ahimelech, escapes and joins David (22:20-23).
David asks the LORD, “Shall I go and attack these Philistines?” and the LORD says, “Go” (23:2).
Jonathan visits David and says, “You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you” (23:16-17).
Saul almost captures David at the wilderness of Maon, but is called away by a Philistine raid (23:26-29).
interpretation:
David’s flight shows that being chosen by God is not the same as being comfortable. He has been anointed king, and he is in a cave. The pattern is clear in many Bible stories: before glory comes hardship, and God uses the wilderness to shape his servants. David was formed as a king in the same years that he was hunted as an outlaw.

His behavior in these chapters is mixed. His lie to Ahimelech has terrible consequences, and David later admits his responsibility: “I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father’s house” (22:22). Scripture does not hide the flaws of its heroes. David is not the model king because he never fails. He is the model because he repents, inquires of the LORD, and clings to God’s promises.

The band that gathers at Adullam is striking. The distressed, the indebted, and the bitter come to him. This is a company of misfits, and David becomes their captain. It is an image of what a faithful king does: he receives those who have nowhere else to go.

The massacre at Nob is one of the darkest scenes in the book. Saul’s own officers refuse to touch the priests, and the Edomite Doeg does it. A king who began with the Spirit of God is now killing the LORD’s priests. The anger that began as envy ends in sacrilege.

Against the darkness, the LORD guides David. Again and again, David inquires through the ephod, and God answers. In chapter 23, the people of Keilah would betray him, but God warns him, and he escapes. Jonathan comes to him “and strengthened his hand in God.” The chapter ends with a narrow escape, which the place name records as “the Rock of Escape.”
connection: Jesus, the Son of David, was also rejected by his own, and in his ministry those in distress, in debt, and bitter of soul gathered to him (Luke 15:1; Matthew 11:28). Jesus cited David’s eating of the bread of the Presence to show that mercy outranks ritual (Matthew 12:3-4). Hebrews 11:38 says of the faithful that they “wandered about in deserts and mountains and in dens and caves of the earth.”
application:
If you are in a wilderness season, remember that God may be forming you.

Ask God for guidance in a decision, as David did, before you act.

Think about who the “distressed, indebted, and bitter” are around you, and how you might welcome them.
prayerPrompts: Tell God about a wilderness where you feel he is forming you.
Thank Jesus for welcoming those who have nowhere else to go.
Ask him to strengthen you in him.
